title: Hello World
subtitle: Words by the Fire
martuIntro:
Hi. It is me, Mar'tu. Before we continue on our adventure, we go back to the first words, yes?
A lot of that campaign code felt like a wall, yes? We will take the wall apart, one stone at a time.
Every spell begins as words. Python is fussy about words. More fussy than Lucky is about glug, yes?
Tonight: how to say something, how to keep something in a box, and how to let Python do the sums.
goals: Show words on the screen with `print()`, in matching quotes
Write `#` notes for humans, and switch a line off
Make a box (variable) with `name = value`, using the exact name the task asks for
Put a new value in a box, like `mana = mana - cost`
Do math with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and let the code combine your boxes
Glue text together with `+` and `str()`, and draw a bar with `"█" * mana`
Read Python's message and mend the slips everyone makes

items.title: How Mar'tu Teaches
items.summary: One minute: how Run, Help and the checkpoints work.
items.body:
Write a line. Press [[run|Run]]. Python answers below.
Pressing Run on unfinished code is allowed and costs nothing. A message from Python is information, not a mark.
Stuck? Press Help. You can always ask for a starting line or more structure.
Checkpoints: ✓ done · ● now · ○ next.
Nothing here is timed. Your hints are private.

items.title: Before the First Spell

exercises.title: What an error looks like
exercises.martu: Press Run first. Then you will break it on purpose and read Python's [[error message|message]]. A message is not a mark against you: it says what Python could not read. Read the last line first: the message under your code shows it as *Python's last line*. Then look at the line it names.

anotherWay.text:
Python's full message, short:
```text
File "main.py", line 1
  print("Shield up.)
        ^
SyntaxError: unterminated ...
```
1. Read the last line first. *Unterminated* means the words never ended: the closing quote is missing.
2. Then the top line: it names the line to mend, line 1.

anotherWay.label: Something everyday
anotherWay.text: It is like a friend saying "I couldn't read the end of your note." They are not upset. They are telling you where to look.

anotherWay.text: Delete the last `"`. Run. Read. Put the `"` back, make the `.` a `!`, and Run.

exercises.title: Where the symbols live
exercises.martu:
Look at the top right of your keyboard:
```text
with Shift:   (   )   _   +
no Shift:     9   0   -   =
```
`-`, `_` and `=` sit side by side. They mean different things. `-` subtracts, `_` joins words in a name, `=` puts a value in a box.

anotherWay.text:
The three keys, circled:
```text
  9   0  (-)  (=)   Backspace
         Shift + (-) gives (_)
```

1. `-` is the key right after `0`.
2. `_` is the same key with Shift held down.
3. `=` is the next key to the right.
4. `"` is Shift with the `'` key, next to Enter.

anotherWay.label: Say it shorter
anotherWay.text: Type `print("`, then the three symbols, then `")`.

exercises.title: Quotes and brackets come in pairs
exercises.martu: [[quotes|Quotes]] come in pairs: one before the words, one after. [[brackets|Brackets]] come in pairs too. This line is missing one. Run it, read the message, then mend it.

anotherWay.text:
Quotes are bookends. Words stand between them:
```text
print("It is not a compass")
     ^^                   ^^
   ( and "           " and )
    open               close
```
The bracket opens first and closes last, around the quotes.

anotherWay.label: Something everyday
anotherWay.text: Shoes come in pairs. One shoe is not a pair. One quote mark is not a pair either.

1. Python finds the first quote and starts reading words.
2. It looks for the next quote, to know where the words stop.
3. It never comes. Python reaches the end of the line and stops: *unterminated*.

anotherWay.label: Say it shorter
anotherWay.text: Line 1 needs a `"`. Line 2 needs a `)`.

exercises.title: Words need quotes
exercises.martu: Words you want to show need [[quotes]]. Without quotes, Python thinks you mean the name of something saved earlier, and it finds nothing.

anotherWay.text:
What Python tries with `print(Fireball)`:
1. No quotes, so this is not words.
2. Then it must be the name of something saved earlier.
3. Python looks for `Fireball`. Nothing is saved with that name.
4. It stops and says *not defined*.

anotherWay.label: Something everyday
anotherWay.text: "Say Lucky" means call Lucky over. "Say 'Lucky'" means say the word. Quotes turn a name into words.

anotherWay.label: This, not this
anotherWay.text:
Not this: `print(Fireball)`. Python looks for a name and finds nothing.
This: `print("Fireball")`. Python shows the word.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? Names versus words
anotherWay.text: Python has two kinds of words. Words in quotes are shown exactly. Words without quotes are names: Python looks them up. `print` itself is a name with no quotes, and Python finds it. `Fireball` is a name with no quotes too, and Python finds nothing.

exercises.title: Top to bottom
exercises.martu: Python runs your lines from top to bottom, one at a time. An empty `print()` shows a blank line.

anotherWay.text:
Read the code like a ladder, top rung first:
```text
line 1  ->  printed first
line 2  ->  printed second
line 3  ->  printed last
```

anotherWay.label: Step table

The finished code, one line at a time:
1. `print("Mar'tu checks the clock.")` shows: Mar'tu checks the clock.
2. `print("The hand is near the arc.")` shows: The hand is near the arc.
3. `print()` shows an empty line.
4. `print("Get inside, yes?")` shows: Get inside, yes?

items.title: Boxes With Labels
items.summary: Keep a value in a labeled box, use the exact name, and change what is inside.

exercises.title: A box with a label
exercises.martu:
A box ([[variable]]) has a label and something inside. `companion = "Gearshift"` makes a box labeled `companion` and puts the text inside. Read `=` as gets: companion gets Gearshift.
```
  companion
+-----------+
| Gearshift |
+-----------+
```

anotherWay.text:
Two lines, two answers:
```
print(companion)
-> opens the box
-> shows Gearshift

print("companion")
-> just the letters
-> shows companion
```

anotherWay.label: Like a phone contact
anotherWay.text: A phone contact has a name with a number saved under it. Tap the name, and the phone uses what is saved. `print(companion)` taps the name. `print("companion")` just reads the word out loud.

anotherWay.label: In Tor
anotherWay.text: A jar on my shelf with a chalk label. The label says `companion`. Inside is Gearshift. Ask for the jar by its label, and you get what is inside.

Python reads one line at a time:
1. `companion = "Gearshift"`: the box `companion` gets Gearshift.
2. `print(companion)`: opens the box and shows Gearshift.
3. `print("companion")`: shows the letters companion.

anotherWay.label: Not this
anotherWay.text:
Not this: `"companion" = "Gearshift"` (a label never goes in quotes). Not this: `companion - "Gearshift"` (`-` subtracts). Not this: a lone `"Gearshift"` (made, then forgotten).
This: `companion = "Gearshift"`.

anotherWay.label: Fill the frame
anotherWay.text: Fill the frame: `____ = ____`. The left blank is the label, with no quotes. The right blank is the value, text in quotes. Like `companion = "Bomb Shell"`.

Read it as: companion gets Gearshift. A box is `name = value`, so `snack = "glug"` makes a box named `snack` with glug inside. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label.

exercises.title: Numbers stand alone
exercises.martu:
Numbers stand alone, with no quotes. `"3"` is text that looks like a [[number]]. `3` is a number Python can do math with.
Lucky says his armor bonus is 30. It is 3. We use the 3.

anotherWay.text:
Two boxes that look alike:
```
armor_bonus = 3
^ a number: Python can
  do math with it

armor_bonus = "3"
^ text: just the letter 3,
  like a word
```

anotherWay.label: A price tag
anotherWay.text: A price tag that says "3" is a label. Three coins in your hand are an amount. Text in quotes is the tag. A number with no quotes is the coins.
Python looks at the value. It sees `3` and makes a number. It sees `"3"` and makes text, because quotes always mean text.

anotherWay.label: Why "3" isn't 3
anotherWay.text: Quotes mean these exact letters. `"3"` is the letter 3, like `"glug"` is the letters g-l-u-g. Python won't do math with letters. Next lesson you will add numbers, so keep them free of quotes.
Words get quotes. Numbers don't.

A box holds one value at a time. Put a new value in, and the old one is gone.
Mana works like this. So does Lucky's glug, sadly.

```

mana:  26  ->  21  ->  14
```

exercises.title: Mar'tu's chalk math
exercises.martu:
Python does math with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. Guess each answer, then run.
These are the [[math signs]]. No quotes around the math, so Python works it out.
My checks are sneaky: they put other numbers in your boxes and run your code again, to see if your line follows. Your own code is not changed. A typed answer can't keep up.

anotherWay.label: Two jars
anotherWay.text:
Two jars and a minus sign:
```text
[ first_gap: 48 ]
        -
[ last_gap: 37 ]
        ->  11
```
Python opens both jars, takes one number from the other, and prints the answer.

anotherWay.label: A calculator that remembers
anotherWay.text: A box is a calculator memory. `first_gap - last_gap` says: take the number saved as first_gap, minus the one saved as last_gap. Change a saved number, and the answer changes with it.

anotherWay.label: The chalk wall
anotherWay.text: My chalk wall: 48, 48, 47, 46, 44, 41, 37. Each number is the hours between two bursts. The first gap was 48. The last was 37. How much did it shrink? 48 take away 37.
`print(first_gap - last_gap)`: two boxes, a minus sign, no quotes.

starter: # Replace 0 with how much the gap shrank, using the two boxes.

checkpoints.text: Replace the `0` so the line prints how much the gap shrank. Use `first_gap` and `last_gap`.

exercises.title: What does each number mean?
exercises.martu:
Before any math, ask two questions about each number: how many? how much is one? Put each number in the box that means that.
A number in the wrong box trips up everyone once. Normal. Now we ask first, yes?

anotherWay.label: Tally marks and a price tag
anotherWay.text:
How many is a row of tally marks. How much is one is a price tag.
```text
lanterns: ||| (3)
price tag: [4 coins]

rope: ||||| (5)
price tag: [2 coins]
```

anotherWay.label: A shopping list
anotherWay.text: A shopping list says '3 lanterns'. The shop's sign says '4 coins each'. The list is how many. The sign is how much one costs. They never swap jobs.

1. Find a number in the story.
2. Ask: is it how many, or how much is one?
3. Put it in the box whose note asks that question.
4. Do the next number.

anotherWay.text: How many jars? How much for one jar? Two questions, two boxes. Ask before you write, yes?

exercises.title: Let the code combine it
exercises.martu:
Do not work the total out yourself. Let Python combine the boxes. Then the total stays right when a number changes.
Some call this [[show your working|showing your working]]. Watch the Example.

anotherWay.label: Arrows into the total
anotherWay.text:
```text
lantern_count * lantern_price
  --> lantern_cost

rope_count * rope_price
  --> rope_cost

lantern_cost + rope_cost
  --> total_cost
```
Change any box on the left, and the arrows carry it all the way to the total.

anotherWay.label: An online cart
anotherWay.text: In an online cart, change the quantity from 3 to 7 and the total updates by itself. That only works because the cart multiplies and adds. It never stores the total as a typed number.

anotherWay.label: Show your working
anotherWay.text: In math class, a teacher wants the working, not just the answer. Python is the same. `total_cost = 22` is just the answer. `total_cost = lantern_cost + rope_cost` is the working, and Python checks it every time it runs.
Cost = how many `*` price of one. Total = cost `+` cost. Never type the answer.

exercises.martu:
`+` [[glue|glues]] text to text. A number must become text first: `str(26)` gives `"26"`. Spaces are text too.
`"Mana: " + 26` makes Python stop: it will not glue text to a number. `"Mana: " + str(26)` works.

anotherWay.text:
Each piece is a bead. Only text beads go on the string. A number needs `str()` to become a bead.
```text
[Lucky] + [ has ] + [26] + [ mana.]
 name     text    str(mana)  text
```

anotherWay.label: A status bar
anotherWay.text:
```text
Oogrish  :   18   /   18   mana
hero_name    mana     max_mana
```

2. `mana = max_mana`, run.
3. `print(hero_name + ": ")`, run.

exercises.title: Repeat a mark
exercises.martu:
`*` also [[stamp|stamps]] text: `"█" * 3` stamps three blocks. A mana bar is full blocks for the mana you have, then light blocks for the mana used.
`+` glues two texts. `*` stamps one text a number of times.

anotherWay.label: A fuel gauge
anotherWay.text:
```text
mana 3 of 5:   [ █ █ █ ░ ░ ]
                 have   used
                 3      5 - 3
```

anotherWay.label: A stamp
anotherWay.text: A rubber stamp makes the same mark again and again. `full * mana` presses the full stamp mana times. `empty * (max_mana - mana)` presses the light stamp once for each point used.

anotherWay.label: What Python does first
anotherWay.text:
For `empty * (max_mana - mana)` with mana 3 of 5:
1. Brackets first: `5 - 3` is 2.
2. Then `empty * 2` stamps `░░`.
Without brackets, Python tries `empty * 5` first, then `"░░░░░" - 3`, and text minus a number is an error.

anotherWay.label: Why brackets?
anotherWay.text: Python does `*` before `-`, just like in math class. Brackets say: do this part first.
Full: `full * mana`. Light: `empty * (max_mana - mana)`. Glue them with `+`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: `get_mana_bar` had `filled = "█" * caster["mana"]` and `empty = "░" * (caster["max_mana"] - caster["mana"])`. Your line is the same bar.

anotherWay.label: Which bug first?
anotherWay.text:
1. Run. Python stops at the first crash and names the line. Mend it.
2. Run again. Mend the next crash.
3. When nothing crashes, the checks speak. Read the message under the step.

anotherWay.text:
```text
loud bugs:
Python stops, and its
message names the line.

quiet bugs:
the program runs, but
the code is wrong.
```

items.summary: Eight questions on quotes, boxes, math and glue. Retake as often as you like.

questions.q: Which line makes a box named `hero` that holds the text Lucky?

whyWrong.0: `def` makes a recipe, not a box.
whyWrong.1: A box's name never goes in quotes.
whyWrong.3: `-` subtracts. To make a box, use `=`.

questions.explain: A box is `name = value`: the name with no quotes, `=`, then the text in quotes.
Each line uses what is in the box now: 18, then 13, then 8. The box keeps only its latest value.

questions.q: This line should show It is not a compass. Mend it.
questions.explain: Quotes come in pairs. Add the closing `"` before the `)`.
`*` stamps each text: two full blocks, then three light blocks, glued with `+`.

questions.q: Fill the blank so this prints `Mana: 7`.
questions.explain: `str(7)` turns the number into text, so it can be glued to `"Mana: "`.

questions.q: Mar'tu changes `lantern_count` to 5. Which `total` line stays right?

whyWrong.0: 22 was worked out by hand for 3 lanterns. It does not change when the count does.
whyWrong.1: 12 was the old lantern cost, typed in. It does not follow the box.
whyWrong.3: 3 is the old count, typed in. Use the box `lantern_count`.

questions.explain: Only the line built from the boxes follows when a box changes. Let the code combine it.

whyWrong.0: The box is named `Health`, with a capital H. `health` is a different name.
whyWrong.1: No quotes, so Python looks for a box named `health`. It does not show the word.

questions.explain: Names are exact, letter for letter. `Health` and `health` are two different names.
Python does `*` before `+`: 5 times 2 is 10, then plus 2 is 12.

items.title: The Night Watch Ledger
items.summary: Mar'tu's ledger for the long night: mana for the barrier, oil for the lanterns, and who keeps watch.
items.intro:
The barrier must hold until the next burst, 37 hours away. Mar'tu keeps a ledger of what the night will cost: mana for the barrier, and flasks of lantern oil.
Three parts, in order: A. what we know, B. let the code combine it, C. write the ledger.
The barrier eats 2 mana an hour. The lanterns burn 1 flask of oil an hour, and a flask costs 3 coins.
items.martu: Thirty-seven hours, yes? I do not want to do these sums by hand at 3 in the morning. Put what we know in boxes, let the code combine them, then write the ledger lines. If the clock changes its mind, the ledger follows.

anotherWay.label: The ledger page
anotherWay.text:
```text
A. what we know
   37 hours, 2 mana/hour,
   1 flask/hour, 3 coins/flask
B. let the code combine it
   mana_needed, oil_needed,
   oil_cost
C. the ledger
   three printed lines
```
Each part only uses boxes from the parts above it.

1. Fill the four boxes in A.
2. In B, multiply: hours times per hour; flasks times price.
3. In C, glue text and `str()` of each box.
4. Run after every line.

anotherWay.label: Why a ledger?
anotherWay.text: The chalk wall says the next burst may come sooner: 32 hours, maybe. If you typed the answers, the whole ledger is wrong. If the code combines them, change one box.

items.title: The Ward Sign
items.summary: Paint TOR down the barrier post in big block letters. One box of ink repaints the whole sign.
items.intro:
Mar'tu wants a ward sign on the barrier post, in big block letters: `TOR`.
Wards work better when they are tidy. Probably.
items.martu:
The post is tall and thin, so the letters go down it, one under another. Each letter is five rows.
Every row uses the box `ink`. Change `ink` once, and the whole sign repaints.
I drew the T. You draw the rest, yes?

anotherWay.label: Squared paper
anotherWay.text:
Draw the letter on squared paper first. Each row of squares is one `print`. A filled square is `ink`. An empty square is a space inside quotes.
```
█████   print(ink * 5)
█   █   print(ink + "   " + ink)
```

anotherWay.label: A stamp pad
anotherWay.text: `ink` is the stamp pad. Every row stamps from it. Swap the pad for a new color once, and every stamp after that is the new color.

1. Look at one row of your letter.
2. Count the marks and the gaps.
3. Write one `print` for that row: marks from `ink`, gaps as spaces in quotes.
4. Run. Then do the next row.
Mar'tu paints wards from one pot of paint. Swap the pot, and the whole sign is a new color. `ink` is the pot. A mark typed straight into a `print` is paint from somewhere else.
One `print` per row. Marks come from `ink`. Gaps are spaces in quotes.

items.title: Clock Math
items.summary: Three more math marks, `**`, `//` and `%`, and the order Python does math in. Then the Ley Clock.
items.body:
Three more math marks. You do not need them for the campaign. They are here for the curious, yes?
1. `**` is a [[power]]: `2 ** 3` means 2 × 2 × 2, which is 8.
2. `//` is [[floor division]]: divide, then keep only the whole part. `50 // 12` is 4.
3. `%` gives the [[remainder]]: what is left over after dividing. `50 % 12` is 2.
Python follows an [[order of operations]]. Brackets first. Then `**`. Then `*`, `/`, `//` and `%`. Then `+` and `-`. So `2 + 3 * 4` is 14, but `(2 + 3) * 4` is 20.
Now the Ley Clock. It has 12 marks, numbered 0 to 11. After mark 11 comes mark 0 again. The hand moves one mark each hour.
The hand is on mark 9. Where is it 50 hours from now? Add first, then wrap: `(9 + 50) % 12` is 11.
The brackets matter. `9 + 7 % 12` does the `%` first and gives 16, which is not even a mark. `(9 + 7) % 12` gives 4.
It is not a compass, Lucky. It is a clock. It goes round.

exercises.title: Where is the hand?
exercises.martu: The Ley Clock has 12 marks, 0 to 11. `% 12` wraps any count back onto the clock. Add first, in brackets. Then wrap.

anotherWay.text:
The marks go round, then start again:
```
... 9 10 11 0 1 2 3 ...
```
Count 5 steps from 10: 11, 0, 1, 2, 3.

anotherWay.label: A wall clock
anotherWay.text: A wall clock does this. Three hours after 11 o'clock is 2 o'clock, not 14 o'clock. `(11 + 3) % 12` is 2.

1. Add: `start + hours`.
2. Too big for the clock? Take away 12, and again, until it fits.
3. What is left is the mark. `% 12` does steps 2 and 3 at once.
`hand = (start + hours) % 12`. Brackets first, then wrap.

items.title: Asking the Traveler: input()
items.summary: Let your program ask a question. The answer is always text, so `int()` turns it into a number.
items.body:
Sometimes a program should ask. The [[input]] command, `input()`, shows a question, called the [[prompt]], and waits for an answer.
Whatever comes back is text. Even `3` comes back as the text `"3"`.
Text cannot do math. `"3" + "3"` glues to `33`. To get a real number, use [[int]]: `int(input("Sips? "))`.
On this site, the answers come from the box called Input for your program, one answer per line. Change them and run again, as often as you like.
You have seen this before. In the campaign, `user.clicked()` handed back text, like `"option 1"`. That is why the dialogue code compared it with words in quotes.

examples.output:
Who knocks? Gearshift
Come in, Gearshift.

items.title: Quick Check 1 · Form A questions
items.summary: Three questions that go with Quick Check 1. Two of three right is a pass.

whyWrong.1: Look at `"] "`: there is a space after the bracket, and spaces are text too.
whyWrong.2: `*` stamps the block 3 times. It does not glue the number on.

questions.explain: `*` stamps: 3 full blocks, 2 empty ones. `"] "` adds the bracket and a space. `str()` turns 3 and 5 into text.
Line 2 takes what is in `x` now (5), takes away 2, and puts 3 back in `x`. A box keeps only its latest value.

questions.q: Which line makes a box whose name Python accepts?

whyWrong.0: A name can't have a space. Python reads two names and stops. Use `_` instead.
whyWrong.2: A box's name never has quotes. Quotes make it text, and text can't be a label.

questions.explain: Names have no spaces and no quotes: `magical_affinity = 9`.

items.title: Quick Check 1 · Form B questions
items.summary: Three questions that go with Quick Check 1. Two of three right is a pass.

whyWrong.1: Look at `"] "`: there is a space after the bracket, and spaces are text too.
whyWrong.2: `*` stamps the block 2 times. It does not glue the number on.

questions.explain: `*` stamps: 2 full blocks, 4 empty ones. `"] "` adds the bracket and a space. `str()` turns 2 and 6 into text.
Line 2 takes what is in `y` now (8), takes away 3, and puts 5 back in `y`. A box keeps only its latest value.

questions.q: Which line makes a box whose name Python accepts?

whyWrong.0: A name can't have a space. Python reads two names and stops. Use `_` instead.
whyWrong.2: A box's name never has quotes. Quotes make it text, and text can't be a label.

questions.explain: Names have no spaces and no quotes: `spell_color = "teal"`. The value can have quotes. The name can't.

items.title: Mar'tu's Chalk Notes: First Words
items.summary: Everything from Unit 1 on one page. Printable.

entries.note: Quotes and brackets come in pairs: one opens, one closes. (Lesson: Words in Quotes)
`print()` with nothing inside prints an empty line.
Python skips any line that starts with `#`. Put `#` in front of a line to switch it off.
A box's name never has quotes. Quotes mean these exact letters. No quotes means look inside the box with this label. (Lesson: Boxes With Labels)
Numbers have no quotes. `"3"` is text that only looks like a number.
Read it as: mana gets mana minus spell cost. The right side runs first, then the answer goes back in the box.
`/` always gives a decimal, like `24.0`. (Lesson: Math and Glue)

entries.concept: How many × how much is one
entries.note: Put each number in a labeled box. Then let the code combine them, so the total follows when a number changes. Never type the total in yourself.
`+` glues text to text. A number must become text first, with `str()`. Spaces are text too.
`+` glues two texts. `*` stamps one text a number of times.
Python does `*` before `-`, so wrap the subtraction in brackets.
SyntaxError: unterminated string literal. Add the missing quote.
SyntaxError: '(' was never closed. Add the missing `)`.

`mana -= 3` is short for `mana = mana - 3`. (Extra practice: The short way)
